question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
She was fond of walking along the path besides the lake.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. besides the lake.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the use of "besides" in place of "beside".

◦ "Beside" is a preposition meaning next to / by the side of, and is used to indicate physical location.

◦ "Besides" is a preposition/adverb meaning in addition to / apart from, and is used to add extra information.

• Since the sentence describes the path running next to the lake (a physical position), the correct preposition is "beside", not "besides".

◦ Example: She sat beside him. (next to him) / Besides singing, she also dances. (in addition to singing)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "along the path" is correct as printed — "along" is the right preposition to show movement over a path.

• Option 3: "She was" is grammatically correct — a simple subject + auxiliary verb construction.

• Option 4: "fond of walking" is correct — "fond of" is correctly followed by a gerund (walking).

NOTE

• Commonly confused preposition pairs tested by SSC: beside/besides, among/between, in/into, on/onto, by/until.

• Remember: beside = next to (place); besides = in addition to (extra info).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Policeman came to my village and asked about a person who burgled a house last night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. policeman.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the word "Policeman" — a common, countable noun used at the start of the sentence without any determiner.

• Rule: A singular countable common noun must be preceded by an article (a/an/the) or another determiner when used in a sentence.

• Since "policeman" refers to one unspecified policeman, it must be preceded by the article "A".

◦ Correct sentence: A policeman came to my village and asked about a person who burgled a house last night.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "a house" is correct — the indefinite article "a" is correctly used before the singular countable noun "house", as it is being mentioned for the first time.

• Option 3: "my village" is correct — the possessive adjective "my" correctly functions as a determiner before "village".

• Option 4: "a person" is correct — the indefinite article "a" is correctly used before the singular countable noun "person", mentioned for the first time.

NOTE

• Singular countable nouns can never stand alone in a sentence — they must always take an article (a/an/the) or another determiner (my, this, some, etc.).

• Common SSC error-spotting trap: missing article before a singular countable noun at the start of a sentence.

question:
Select the option that will improve the given sentence by using the most appropriate verb.
Soorya walking to college every day.
option_1: Soorya is walking to college every day.
option_2: Soorya walked to college every day.
option_3: Soorya walk to college every day.
option_4: Soorya have walked to college every day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Soorya walked to college every day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Soorya walking to college every day" is grammatically incomplete because the -ing form (present participle) "walking" cannot function as the main verb of a sentence without a helping/auxiliary verb.

• Rule: A bare V-ing form needs an auxiliary verb (is/am/are/was/were) to work as the main verb, or it must be replaced by a finite verb form that agrees correctly with the subject.

• Among the given choices, "walked" (Simple Past Tense, V2 form) makes the sentence a complete, grammatically correct, and meaningful statement, while all the other options contain a further grammatical flaw of their own (explained below).

◦ Structure: Subject + V2 (+ Object) + Adverbial of time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Soorya is walking to college every day" is grammatically complete but semantically odd — the Present Continuous Tense ("is walking") is normally used for an action happening right now or a temporary arrangement, and does not naturally combine with the habitual time marker "every day".

• Option 3: "Soorya walk to college every day" is incorrect because it lacks subject-verb agreement — a third-person singular subject (Soorya) in the Simple Present Tense requires the verb to take an "-s/-es" ending (walks), not the bare form "walk".

• Option 4: "Soorya have walked to college every day" is incorrect because of a subject-verb agreement error — a third-person singular subject requires the auxiliary "has", not "have", in the Present Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• A bare present participle (V-ing) can never be the main verb of a finite sentence on its own; it always needs a helping verb.

• Subject-verb agreement rule: third-person singular subjects (he/she/it/singular noun) take "-s/-es" in Simple Present and "has" in Present Perfect.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error mark 'No error' as your answer.
Father took the newspaper / in his hand to / go through it once again.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Father took the newspaper in his hand to go through it once again" is grammatically correct in every part.

• "Father took the newspaper" — correct Simple Past Tense construction (Subject + V2 + Object).

• "in his hand to" — correctly shows the manner of holding the newspaper, followed by the infinitive "to" showing purpose.

• "go through it once again" — "go through" is a correctly used phrasal verb meaning to read/examine, followed by the object "it" and the adverbial "once again".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in his hand to" contains no error — it is a correct prepositional and infinitive phrase.

• Option 2: "Father took the newspaper" contains no error — correct subject-verb-object structure in Simple Past Tense.

• Option 3: "go through it once again" contains no error — "go through" correctly means to read carefully, and the object pronoun "it" correctly refers back to "the newspaper".

NOTE

• In error-spotting questions, always check each segment individually for subject-verb agreement, tense, preposition usage, and article usage before concluding "No error".

• The phrasal verb "go through" has multiple meanings depending on context: to examine/read (as here), to experience (a difficulty), or to be approved (a proposal).

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

What is literacy? It is the golden key that (1)________ the gates to a whole new world. It heralds the dawn of a new (2)________. But the media hype seems to give the impression that literacy simply means the ability to sign one's name, instead of putting thumb impression. Isn't that a very (3)________, simplistic interpretation of the word?
Taking up this narrow meaning of the word, politicians proclaim that their states have achieved 80 or 90 per cent literacy or even (4)________. But quite often, what happens is, once the training course is over, to produce (5)________, the neo-literates soon lapse into illiteracy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. opens.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage uses the extended metaphor of literacy as a "golden key". A key's basic function is to open a lock/gate, so the verb that logically completes **"the golden key that _____ the gates to a whole new world" is "opens"**.

• The verb must agree with the singular relative pronoun "that" referring back to "key" (third person singular), so the correct form is "opens", not "open".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "closes" is incorrect — it is the opposite of what a key metaphorically does to open access to a "new world"; it contradicts the positive sense of the passage.

• Option 3: "controls" is incorrect — while a key can be loosely associated with access, "controls the gates" does not fit the established idiom of a "key opening" something.

• Option 4: "leads" is incorrect — a key does not grammatically or idiomatically "lead" gates; keys are said to "open" locks/gates/doors.

NOTE

• Common collocations with "key": key opens a door/gate, key to success, turn the key.

• In cloze passages, always look for fixed collocations and idiomatic verb-noun pairings rather than just literal meaning.

But the media hype seems to give the impression that literacy simply means the ability to sign one's name, instead of putting thumb impression. Isn't that a very (3)________, simplistic interpretation of the word?
Taking up this narrow meaning of the word, politicians proclaim that their states have achieved 80 or 90 per cent literacy or even (4)________. But quite often, what happens is, once the training course is over, to produce (5)________, the neo-literates soon lapse into illiteracy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states that literacy **"heralds the dawn of a new ____". The word "dawn" collocates naturally with "day" — "the dawn of a new day"** is a well-established fixed expression signifying a fresh beginning.

• Collocation rule: "dawn of a new ___" conventionally pairs with day (or, figuratively, "era"), not with year, month, or season.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "year" is incorrect — "dawn of a new year" is not the standard idiomatic collocation used here; the passage's imagery (golden key, gates, dawn) works with the smaller, more immediate unit "day".

• Option 3: "month" is incorrect — "dawn of a new month" is not an established or natural collocation in English.

• Option 4: "season" is incorrect — "dawn of a new season" is not idiomatic; dawn is associated with a single day, not a season.

NOTE

• Fixed expression to remember for SSC vocabulary/cloze questions: "the dawn of a new day/era" — signifies a fresh start or new beginning.

• Distinguish "dawn" (literal: sunrise; figurative: beginning) from words like "onset", "advent", and "outset", which are near-synonyms tested in vocabulary sections.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

What is literacy? It is the golden key that (1)________ the gates to a whole new world. It heralds the dawn of a new (2)________. But the media hype seems to give the impression that literacy simply means the ability to sign one's name, instead of putting thumb impression. Isn't that a very (3)________, simplistic interpretation of the word?
Taking up this narrow meaning of the word, politicians proclaim that their states have achieved 80 or 90 per cent literacy or even (4)________. But quite often, what happens is, once the training course is over, to produce (5)________, the neo-literates soon lapse into illiteracy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. limited.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the media's narrow understanding of literacy (equating it merely with the ability to sign one's name). The word must be a near-synonym of "simplistic", since the sentence itself pairs the blank with ", simplistic interpretation".

• "Limited" means restricted in scope or extent, which logically matches a narrow, oversimplified understanding of literacy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "daunted" is incorrect — "daunted" means intimidated/discouraged, which does not describe an "interpretation" of a word; it is a mismatched part of speech/meaning for this context.

• Option 3: "wide" is incorrect — it is the opposite in sense; the passage is criticising the media for taking a narrow view, not a wide one.

• Option 4: "small" is incorrect — while "small" is not entirely illogical, it does not collocate as naturally with "interpretation" as "limited" does, and is a weaker fit than "limited" in formal usage.

NOTE

• In cloze tests, always check the immediate co-text (the word/phrase right before or after the blank) — here, the following word "simplistic" is the biggest clue, since the passage is building a pair of similar, reinforcing adjectives.

• Synonyms of "limited" useful for SSC vocabulary: restricted, narrow, confined, constrained.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

What is literacy? It is the golden key that (1)________ the gates to a whole new world. It heralds the dawn of a new (2)________. But the media hype seems to give the impression that literacy simply means the ability to sign one's name, instead of putting thumb impression. Isn't that a very (3)________, simplistic interpretation of the word?
Taking up this narrow meaning of the word, politicians proclaim that their states have achieved 80 or 90 per cent literacy or even (4)________. But quite often, what happens is, once the training course is over, to produce (5)________, the neo-literates soon lapse into illiteracy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. higher.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"politicians proclaim that their states have achieved 80 or 90 per cent literacy or even ____."** The blank must logically continue the idea of an increasing figure beyond "80 or 90 per cent".

• "Higher" correctly conveys the idea of an even greater percentage than the ones already mentioned (i.e., approaching 100 per cent).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "better" is incorrect — "better" describes quality, not a numerical percentage; it does not logically follow "80 or 90 per cent... or even ____" which requires a comparative of quantity.

• Option 3: "lower" is incorrect — it contradicts the boastful tone of politicians exaggerating their achievement; a lower percentage would undercut their claim.

• Option 4: "moderate" is incorrect — "moderate" suggests an average or middling figure, which contradicts the sense of exaggerated, escalating claims implied by "or even ____" after already high figures (80-90%).

NOTE

• In cloze passages involving numbers/percentages, look for words that logically continue a scale (higher/lower/more/less) rather than descriptive adjectives (better/moderate).

• The phrase "or even ___" typically introduces an extreme or exaggerated extension of the idea just stated.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

What is literacy? It is the golden key that (1)________ the gates to a whole new world. It heralds the dawn of a new (2)________. But the media hype seems to give the impression that literacy simply means the ability to sign one's name, instead of putting thumb impression. Isn't that a very (3)________, simplistic interpretation of the word?
Taking up this narrow meaning of the word, politicians proclaim that their states have achieved 80 or 90 per cent literacy or even (4)________. But quite often, what happens is, once the training course is over, to produce (5)________, the neo-literates soon lapse into illiteracy.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. literates.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"once the training course is over, to produce ____, the neo-literates soon lapse into illiteracy." The blank must name the direct outcome/product of a literacy training course, which the next clause then refers to as "the neo-literates"**.

• "Literates" (people who can read and write) is the correct word, since the following clause explicitly calls them "the neo-literates" — i.e., newly made literates — confirming that the training course's product is literate persons.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "education" is incorrect — a training course produces literate people, not "education" itself; "education" cannot logically be the antecedent that the next clause calls "the neo-literates".

• Option 3: "beginners" is incorrect — "beginners" does not specifically capture the sense of newly acquired literacy; the passage specifically discusses literacy/illiteracy, not general skill levels.

• Option 4: "pupils" is incorrect — "pupils" refers to students in general, not specifically to people who have just become literate; it does not connect logically to "neo-literates" in the following clause.

NOTE

• The prefix "neo-" means "new" — e.g., neo-literate (newly literate), neo-classical (new classical style), neo-natal (newborn).

• Always match a cloze blank with pronoun/noun references in the surrounding sentences — here, "the neo-literates" is the biggest clue confirming "literates" as the answer.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Magnificent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Splendid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Magnificent" means extremely beautiful, elaborate, or impressive; grand in appearance. (शानदार/भव्य)

◦ Example: The palace had a magnificent view of the valley.

• "Splendid" means magnificent, very impressive, or excellent, making it the closest synonym. (भव्य/शानदार)

◦ Example: They stayed in a splendid hotel overlooking the sea.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Modest" (विनम्र/साधारण): Unassuming or not very large/impressive — this is nearly an antonym, not a synonym, of "magnificent".

• Option 2: "Regular" (नियमित/साधारण): Usual, normal, or ordinary — the opposite sense of the grandeur implied by "magnificent".

• Option 3: "Humble" (विनम्र): Having a modest or low estimate of one's own importance — again close to an antonym of "magnificent".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "magnificent" useful for SSC: grand, majestic, glorious, sumptuous, resplendent.

• Antonyms of "magnificent": modest, plain, humble, ordinary.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Indigenous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Aboriginal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Indigenous" means originating or occurring naturally in a particular place; native. (मूल निवासी/स्वदेशी)

◦ Example: Kangaroos are indigenous to Australia.

• "Aboriginal" means native to a place; an original inhabitant, making it the closest synonym. (आदिवासी/मूल निवासी)

◦ Example: The aboriginal tribes of the region have lived there for centuries.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Artificial" (कृत्रिम): Made by humans, not occurring naturally — this is the opposite of "indigenous".

• Option 3: "Tangible" (मूर्त/स्पर्शनीय): Able to be touched or physically perceived — unrelated in meaning to "indigenous".

• Option 4: "Literary" (साहित्यिक): Relating to literature or written works — unrelated in meaning to "indigenous".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "indigenous": native, local, domestic, endemic.

• Antonyms of "indigenous": foreign, alien, exotic, imported.

question:
Select the most appropriate spelling of the underlined word in the given sentence.
He lost all senisation in his legs through a cramp.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. sensation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "sensation" — a physical feeling or perception (e.g., in the body), or a state of excited public interest.

◦ Example: He lost all sensation in his legs through a cramp.

• Spelling key: SENS + ATION. The word derives from the Latin "sensus" (feeling), and the noun-forming suffix "-ation" is added directly after "sens-", with a single "s" and no extra vowels inserted.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "syansation" — incorrect; the letters "y" and "a" have been wrongly inserted after "S".

• Option 2: "sensition" — incorrect; the middle vowel should be "a" ("sensation"), not "i" ("sensition").

• Option 3: "sansation" — incorrect; the first vowel should be "e" ("sensation"), not "a" ("sansation").

NOTE

• Related word forms: sense (noun/verb), sensory (adjective), sensational (adjective), sensitive (adjective) — do not confuse these with "sensation".

• Commonly misspelt "-ation" words in SSC exams: information, imagination, communication, presentation.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
When Serena / will arrive, / she will / call you.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. will arrive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence contains a subordinate clause of time introduced by "When", followed by a main clause "she will call you".

• Rule — clauses of time/condition: When a sentence has a main clause in the Future Tense, the subordinate clause beginning with time/conditional conjunctions (when, if, as soon as, before, after, till, until) must be in the Simple Present Tense, not the Future Tense.

• Applying the rule: "will arrive" in the time clause must be changed to the Simple Present "arrives".

◦ Correct sentence: When Serena arrives, she will call you.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "call you" is correct — it correctly completes the main clause "she will call you" in the Future Simple Tense.

• Option 3: "she will" is correct — the subject "she" and the future auxiliary "will" are correctly used in the main clause.

• Option 4: "When Serena" is correct — it correctly introduces the time clause with the subject "Serena".

NOTE

• This rule also applies to conditional (if) clauses: "If it rains, we will stay home" (NOT "If it will rain...").

• Other time conjunctions that follow this rule: before, after, till/until, as soon as, once, by the time.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A sting in the tail
option_1: An unexpected, typically unpleasant or problematic end to something
option_2: Something which seems bad at first but contains a pleasant part at the end
option_3: To initiate a situation that is very complicated or problematic
option_4: A situation in which a large group has to do something to satisfy a small group
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. An unexpected, typically unpleasant or problematic end to something.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A sting in the tail" means an unexpected and unpleasant twist or problem that comes at the end of something that otherwise seemed fine. (अंत में अप्रत्याशित रूप से आने वाली परेशानी)

◦ Example: The deal looked profitable, but there was a sting in the tail — huge hidden fees.

• The idiom comes from creatures like scorpions, whose dangerous sting is located at the end of their tail — hence the association with a hidden, unpleasant surprise appearing right at the very end.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Something which seems bad at first but contains a pleasant part at the end" (उलटा अर्थ): This describes the opposite idea — a pleasant twist, not the meaning of "a sting in the tail".

• Option 3: "To initiate a situation that is very complicated or problematic" (जटिल स्थिति शुरू करना): This matches idioms like "open a can of worms", not "a sting in the tail".

• Option 4: "A situation in which a large group has to do something to satisfy a small group" (बहुसंख्यक को अल्पसंख्यक हेतु कार्य करना): This is unrelated in meaning to "a sting in the tail".

NOTE

• Other idioms with animal/insect imagery tested in SSC: "a fly in the ointment" (a small flaw that spoils something), "a snake in the grass" (a hidden danger/treacherous person), "kill two birds with one stone" (to achieve two things at once).

• Idioms about unpleasant surprises: "a bolt from the blue", "a rude awakening".

question:
Identify the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
To avoid indigetion, it is necessary to chew food properly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. indigetion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "indigestion" — a condition of difficulty in digesting food, often causing discomfort in the stomach.

◦ Example: He suffered from indigestion after eating too fast.

• Spelling key: IN + DI + GEST + ION. The word is built from the prefix "in-" (not), the root "digest" (to break down food), and the suffix "-ion". The word printed in the sentence, "indigetion", wrongly drops the letter "s" from the root "digest".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "chew" is correctly spelt — meaning to crush food with the teeth.

• Option 2: "necessary" is correctly spelt — remember the pattern "one c, two s's" (ne-c-ess-ary).

• Option 3: "properly" is correctly spelt — the adverb form of "proper" formed by adding "-ly".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "indigestion" (difficulty digesting food) with "indigenous" (native) or "ingestion" (the act of consuming food) — these are commonly confused in SSC vocabulary/spelling questions.

• Other frequently misspelt "-tion" words in SSC exams: suggestion, exaggeration, congestion, digestion.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.
The interdisciplinary approach utilised in this study facilitates comprehensive understanding of the complex phenomenon under investigation.
option_2: will have facilitated a comprehensive understanding
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. facilitated a comprehensive understanding.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined portion "facilitates comprehensive understanding" is faulty because the noun "understanding" is used here as a singular countable noun and needs the article "a" before it, and the sentence's overall context (describing a study using the phrase "utilised in this study") calls for a consistent Simple Past Tense verb.

• Rule: A singular countable noun such as "understanding" (in the sense of "an understanding/interpretation") must be preceded by an article; and verbs describing completed research actions in formal/academic writing are conventionally reported in the Simple Past Tense.

• Replacing "facilitates" with "facilitated" and adding the article "a" before "comprehensive understanding" corrects both errors and keeps the sentence grammatically consistent and meaningful.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "will have facilitated a comprehensive understanding" is incorrect — the Future Perfect Tense is illogical here, as the study and its approach are already completed/ongoing, not a future event.

• Option 3: "utilises a comprehensive understanding" is incorrect — semantically, one cannot "utilise an understanding" in this context; the verb "utilises" does not logically pair with "understanding" as its object here.

• Option 4: "is facilitates a comprehensive understanding" is incorrect — it wrongly combines the auxiliary "is" with the finite verb "facilitates", producing an invalid double-verb construction.

NOTE

• Academic/formal writing describing completed research typically uses the Simple Past Tense to report what was done and found.

• Singular countable nouns (understanding, approach, analysis, when used in countable senses) require an article (a/an/the) before them.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Abandon
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Adopt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Abandon" means to give up completely, desert, or leave behind permanently. (त्यागना/छोड़ देना)

◦ Example: They had to abandon the ship as it began to sink.

• "Adopt" means to take up or embrace (a course of action, idea, or child) formally, making it the direct opposite of giving something up. (अपनाना/ग्रहण करना)

◦ Example: The company decided to adopt a new policy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Randomize" (यादृच्छिक बनाना): To arrange something in a random order — unrelated in meaning to "abandon".

• Option 3: "Destroy" (नष्ट करना): To damage something so badly it no longer exists — close in tone to "abandon" but not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Surrender" (आत्मसमर्पण करना): To give oneself up or stop resisting — a near-synonym, not an antonym, of "abandon".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "abandon": desert, forsake, relinquish, discard.

• Other antonyms of "abandon": retain, keep, maintain, preserve.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Gift of the gab
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Talent for speaking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Gift of the gab" means a natural talent or skill in speaking fluently, confidently, and persuasively. (वाक्पटुता/बोलने की सहज कला)

◦ Example: As a salesman, he has the gift of the gab and can convince anyone to buy his products.

• The word "gab" is an informal term for talk/chatter, and calling it a "gift" emphasises that this ability to talk smoothly is viewed as a natural, inborn skill.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Witty" (वाक्चातुर्य युक्त): Describes cleverness in a quick, humorous way of speaking — related, but not the actual meaning of the idiom, which is about fluency of speech in general, not humour.

• Option 2: "Humorous" (हास्यपूर्ण): Refers to having a comedic quality — this is not what "gift of the gab" specifically denotes.

• Option 4: "Talent for singing" (गायन की प्रतिभा): Refers to musical ability, which is unrelated to "gab" (talk).

NOTE

• Other idioms about speaking ability tested in SSC: "silver-tongued" (persuasive/eloquent in speech), "to talk the hind legs off a donkey" (to talk excessively).

• Do not confuse "gift of the gab" (talking ability) with "a way with words" (skill in writing/using language elegantly).

question:
Select the most appropriate collocation to fill in the blank.
Ujjwal was imprisoned for ________ a crime.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. committing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct collocation with "crime" is "to commit a crime", meaning to carry out or perpetrate an unlawful act.

• Rule — fixed collocations: Certain nouns pair conventionally with specific verbs in English; "crime" always collocates with "commit", regardless of other verbs that might seem logically similar.

◦ Example: He was arrested for committing theft.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "making" is incorrect — "making a crime" is not an accepted English collocation.

• Option 2: "undertaking" is incorrect — "undertaking a crime" is not a standard, natural collocation in English.

• Option 4: "involving" is incorrect — "involving a crime" does not function correctly in this context; "involve" requires a different sentence structure (e.g., "a case involving a crime").

NOTE

• Other common "commit" collocations: commit a crime/an offence/a mistake/suicide/an error.

• Similarly fixed collocations frequently tested by SSC: "make a decision", "take a risk", "pay attention", "do damage".

question:
Identify the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
He worked alone as he did not want anyone to hamper his project.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Help.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hamper" means to hinder, obstruct, or make it difficult for something to progress. (बाधा डालना/रोकना)

◦ Example: Heavy rain hampered the rescue operation.

• "Help" means to assist or make it easier for someone to do something or for something to progress, making it the direct opposite of "hamper". (सहायता करना)

◦ Example: She helped him finish the project on time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Care" (देखभाल करना): Means to look after or feel concern for someone/something — unrelated in meaning to "hamper".

• Option 3: "Impede" (बाधा डालना): Means to delay or obstruct — this is a synonym, not an antonym, of "hamper".

• Option 4: "Finish" (समाप्त करना): Means to complete or bring to an end — not the direct opposite of "hamper" (which concerns hindrance, not completion).

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "hamper": hinder, obstruct, impede, hold back, encumber.

• Other antonyms of "hamper": assist, facilitate, aid, ease, further.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
He is not friendly with him in the office.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Hostile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Friendly" means kind, warm, and pleasant in one's behaviour towards others. (मित्रतापूर्ण/मैत्रीपूर्ण)

◦ Example: She gave a friendly smile to the new employee.

• "Hostile" means unfriendly, antagonistic, or showing ill will towards someone, making it the direct opposite of "friendly". (शत्रुतापूर्ण/विरोधी)

◦ Example: The two neighbours have had a hostile relationship for years.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Revel" (मौज-मस्ती करना): A verb meaning to enjoy oneself in a lively, uninhibited way — unrelated in meaning to "friendly".

• Option 3: "Gregarious" (मिलनसार): Means sociable, fond of company — this is a synonym, not an antonym, of "friendly".

• Option 4: "Intelligent" (बुद्धिमान): Relates to mental ability, not to social warmth — unrelated in meaning to "friendly".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "friendly": amiable, cordial, affable, sociable, genial.

• Other antonyms of "friendly": unfriendly, antagonistic, aloof, cold, unsociable.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
No sooner did we reach at the party that it began to rain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. than it began to rain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the correlative construction "No sooner... than...", which is used to describe two actions happening in very quick succession — as soon as one action is completed, the other happens.

• Rule — correlative conjunction: "No sooner" must always be paired with "than", never with "that", "before", or "as".

◦ Structure: No sooner + had/did + Subject + V1/V3 ... + than + Subject + V2 ...

◦ Example: No sooner had he reached the station than the train left.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "it began to rain" is incorrect — it drops the required correlative conjunction entirely, leaving the sentence structurally incomplete.

• Option 2: "before it began to rain" is incorrect — "before" does not pair with "no sooner" as a fixed correlative; it also disturbs the intended meaning of near-simultaneous events.

• Option 4: "as it began to rain" is incorrect — "as" does not form the correct correlative pair with "no sooner"; only "than" is grammatically accepted.

NOTE

• Other fixed correlative conjunction pairs tested by SSC: "hardly/scarcely... when/before...", "not only... but also...", "either... or...", "neither... nor...".

• Remember: "No sooner" and "hardly/scarcely" trigger inversion of subject and auxiliary when placed at the start of a sentence (e.g., "No sooner did he arrive...").

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
I cannot use my office at the moment because it being painted.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. it is being painted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "it being painted" is grammatically incomplete — the present participle "being painted" cannot function as the main verb of the clause without a helping/auxiliary verb.

• Rule — Present Continuous Passive Voice: Subject + is/am/are + being + V3 (past participle). Since the action (painting the office) is happening currently ("at the moment"), the Present Continuous Passive is required.

• Adding the auxiliary "is" (agreeing with the singular subject "it") correctly completes the clause: "it is being painted".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "it had been paint" is incorrect — it uses the Past Perfect auxiliary "had been" with the base form "paint" instead of the past participle "painted", making it doubly ungrammatical, and it is also the wrong tense for a currently ongoing action.

• Option 3: "it has being painted" is incorrect — it wrongly combines the Present Perfect auxiliary "has" with "being" (a continuous marker); the correct continuous passive requires "is/am/are being + V3", not "has being + V3".

• Option 4: "No substitution required" is incorrect because the original segment "it being painted" is grammatically incomplete and does require correction.

NOTE

• Present Continuous Passive structure: is/am/are + being + V3 (e.g., The road is being repaired).

• Present Perfect Passive structure (for comparison): has/have + been + V3 (e.g., The road has been repaired) — do not mix these two structures.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of 'amazement' to fill the blank.
Leena was filled with ________ when she saw the diamond ring as her wedding gift.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. astonishment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Amazement" means a feeling of great surprise or wonder. (आश्चर्य/अचंभा)

◦ Example: He looked at the magician's trick with amazement.

• "Astonishment" means a feeling of great surprise, similar to amazement, making it the closest synonym that also fits the sentence context of receiving an unexpected, impressive gift. (चकित होना/आश्चर्यचकित होना)

◦ Example: She was filled with astonishment on seeing the surprise party.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "happiness" (खुशी): Means a feeling of joy or contentment — while Leena may also feel happy, "happiness" does not capture the specific sense of surprise conveyed by "amazement".

• Option 2: "measurement" (माप): Refers to the size, quantity, or extent of something as ascertained by measuring — completely unrelated to "amazement".

• Option 3: "haughtiness" (घमंड): Means arrogance or a sense of superiority — unrelated in meaning to "amazement".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "amazement": wonder, awe, surprise, bewilderment.

• Antonyms of "amazement": indifference, calmness, boredom.

question:
Select the most appropriate pair of words to fill in the blanks.
Yesterday, he ________ pizza and ________ burgers in one go.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. ate; eight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires two different homophones: "ate" (the past tense of the verb "eat") for the first blank, and "eight" (the number 8) for the second blank.

• First blank: The sentence needs a verb showing the past action of eating pizza — "ate" (Simple Past Tense of "eat").

• Second blank: The sentence needs a number specifying how many burgers he consumed — "eight" (the numeral).

◦ Correct sentence: Yesterday, he ate pizza and eight burgers in one go.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "eight; ate" is incorrect — the words are reversed; "eight" cannot function as a verb, and "ate" cannot function as a number of burgers.

• Option 2: "ate; ate" is incorrect — the second blank needs the number "eight" (how many burgers), not the verb "ate" repeated, which produces a meaningless/incomplete idea of quantity.

• Option 3: "eight; eight" is incorrect — the first blank needs a verb ("ate") to describe the action of eating pizza; "eight" is a number and cannot function as the main verb of the clause.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophones tested by SSC: ate/eight, be/bee, sea/see, hear/here, right/write, their/there/they're.

• A quick trick to distinguish: "eight" is spelt with "eigh" like the number "weight"/"height", while "ate" simply rhymes with "gate/late" and functions as a verb.
